Commission reporting

Follow one ticket payment from a sales record to a payable commission. Change the payment, rule, or hold to see which number moves.

One payment, five decisions

A $600 season plan belongs to Casey at Harbor. A $240 payment arrives on August 5. The example policy deducts $30 in components from each allocation and pays 8% for plans covering six or more games.

  1. Match a rule
    6 games → 8%Plan length is the game count, not the number of seats.
  2. Allocate cash
    $240.00$360.00 of the ticket remains unpaid.
  3. Deduct components
    $210.00 commissionableThe synthetic policy deducts $30 from this allocation.
  4. Calculate
    $16.80 calculated$210.00 × 8% = $16.80.
  5. Release to report
    $16.80 payableAugust · payment date August 5.

Calculated and payable agree because this allocation is not on hold.

A hold changes what is payable. It preserves the calculated amount so a reviewer can explain the difference. An unmatched rule needs review before a payout can be calculated.

Where the number comes from

Ticket + payment
→
Warehouse rules
→
Commission rows
→
Report + review

The ticketing system provides the sale and cash received. Warehouse transformations match the product, team, period, and rate. Finance reviews the resulting rows before payroll uses an approved export.

The row a reviewer needs
QuestionEvidence
Which sale and payment?Stable ticket ID and payment allocation ID
Why this rate?Matched rule, product, game count, and effective period
Why this month?Payment date for plans; event date for group tickets in this example
Why is payable lower?Hold status and reason, beside the calculated amount

Three teams, three rulebooks

A common reporting shape can support different business policies. The rule table keeps those differences visible instead of burying them in a report formula.

Example teamRule keyIllustrative rate
HarborProduct + game count6+ games → 8%
SummitProduct + sales codeNew plan → 9%
ValleySeason + seller levelSenior seller → 10%
What this example leaves configurable

Rates, deductions, split credit, reversals, and date rules are business policy. The $30 deduction here is per allocation: a second $360 allocation would calculate $26.40, for $43.20 total. A once-per-ticket deduction would produce a different total. A real rulebook must name that grain explicitly.
